newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Wartime Swedish government soft on Nazi gold-media.
newsitem.headline: Wartime Swedish government soft on Nazi gold-media.

text.p: The Swedish government during World War Two put pressure on the country's central bank not too ask too many questions about the origins of gold emanating from Nazi Germany, Swedish media reported on Tuesday.

Daily newspaper Dagens Nyheter and Swedish radio said in a jointly produced report that the government complicity was discovered in memorandums at the Riksbank (Central Bank) archives written in 1943 and discovered by their reporters.
Sweden's policy during the war has come under scrutiny following criticism of Swiss banks' dealings with Nazi Germany.

Both countries were neutral. Sweden maintained extensive trade ties with Germay during the war, selling it large amounts of iron ore. German troops transited through Sweden -- with official approval -- to neighbouring Norway, which was invaded.
In return for the ore, Sweden was paid with gold that some historians now say may have been looted from Jews or from occupied countries.
The Swedish Riksbank has agreed to open its archives to historians researching the issue.
Sweden returned about 13 tonnes of gold to Belgium and the Netherlands after the war when it was shown it had been looted by occupying Germans.

The latest report said wartime central bank governor Ivar Rooth expressed concern in February, 1943, to Trade Minister Herman Eriksson about allied threats to demand compensation after the war if it was shown that neutral governments had bought looted Nazi gold.

"I requested that the question on the continuation of the gold trade should be taken up with Emil Puhl (deputy head of Germany's Reichsbank)...I wanted to draw Puhl's attention to the English statements and win an assurance that -- to avoid unpleasantness and loss for the central bank -- that the Reichsbank should declare itself prepared to deliver only gold that was not covered by the allied governments' declarations."
Dagens Nyheter said Sweden's Central Bank had apparently never previously considered the possibility that the gold it received as payment may have been looted.

In a reply that would be damaging to Sweden's already tarnished history during World War Two if the newly published documents are authenticated, the trade minister replied -- in two separate memos -- that Rooth should not concern himself with the origins of the German gold.
"The government held the unanimous view that there was not sufficient grounds to take up the issues in any of the ways I had proposed," Rooth wrote.
Another memo urged Rooth to do his utmost to meet Germany's requests for more gold trade.
Not reassured, Rooth took the matter up with the governing board of the central bank, which ruled that the government should take up the matter more seriously with the central bank.
Germany subsequently reassured Sweden that the gold it was using for payment was not looted, a statement used frequently for the rest of the war to justify continued Swedish purchases.

Sweden only decided in March, 1944, a year before the end of the war and months before allied troops launched the invasion of France, to stop accepting German gold in return for the 35 million tonnes of Swedish iron ore.
